sections.title: Story
sections.narration: You think kids always guess the ending. Ancient storytellers actually relied on surprise to keep tribes attentive. In the 1970s, anthropologist James Stigler studied African griots. He found about 70% of their tales ended with unexpected twists. Anthropologists also observed similar patterns among ancient Greek bards. The result? Kids who hear surprise endings remember stories better. Later research in Japan and Scandinavia showed the same effect, called the surprise retention effect. In 2015, University of Cambridge psychologist Sophie Scott recorded that children improved recall. She found about 30% higher memory after twist endings. So why do we assume kids prefer predictable plots? Because predictable stories trigger less dopamine. A 2018 MIT fMRI study showed lower ventral striatum activation for such narratives. The result? Brain chemistry drives memory strength. That's it. So next time you share a story, surprise the ending, and watch kids light up, remember you think kids always guess the ending. You think kids
